overview: Edmontosaurus regalis and E. annectens were among the largest hadrosaurs, reaching 12–13 metres and up to 4 tonnes, from the latest Cretaceous of North America (~73–66 Ma). A remarkable "Edmontosaurus mummy" — with extensive skin and soft-tissue preservation including a fleshy crest on the head — provided unprecedented detail about hadrosaur integument and revealed a cock's-comb-like structure not visible in the skeleton alone.

Edmontosaurus was the most abundant large herbivore at the very end of the Cretaceous, sharing its world with Tyrannosaurus and Triceratops. Bite marks on Edmontosaurus tail vertebrae from a large tyrannosaur — and a healed tail that shows the animal survived the attack — provide direct evidence of sublethal predator-prey interaction between T. rex and its most common prey.

articles.title: The mummies
articles.body: At least three Edmontosaurus specimens preserve extensive skin and soft tissue — more than any other non-avian dinosaur genus. The most complete (AMNH 5060, "Trachodon mummy") was collected by Charles Sternberg's sons in 1908 and shows desiccated skin, tendons and the impression of a fleshy crest on the skull. A 2013 specimen revealed a rounded cock's-comb-like structure on the head, completely invisible in skeletal material.

articles.title: T. rex predation evidence
articles.body: A tail vertebra of Edmontosaurus bears a puncture wound matching large tyrannosaur tooth size, and the surrounding bone shows extensive healing — the hadrosaur survived. This is the clearest published example of a sublethal T. rex attack on a large herbivore and confirms that T. rex did actively hunt healthy prey rather than only scavenge.

articles.title: Hadrosaur dental batteries
articles.body: Edmontosaurus had hundreds of teeth arranged in a grinding battery — up to 60 teeth stacked in each position with replacements developing below. This system could efficiently process the tough conifer vegetation of the Late Cretaceous. The grinding surface produced by the battery resembles a millstone in function, processing large volumes of plant material rapidly.

record.mya: late Campanian-early Maastrichtian, roughly 73-69 million years ago for E. regalis
record.description: Edmontosaurus regalis was a large, broad-beaked saurolophine hadrosaurid from the Horseshoe Canyon and equivalent formations of Canada. Numerous skulls and skeletons across growth stages document its anatomy; later Maastrichtian E. annectens is a separate species and should not be blended into one undifferentiated profile.
facts: Multiple specimens preserve skin impressions, and one Edmontosaurus specimen preserves a fleshy head comb.
Dental batteries and wear surfaces document sophisticated plant processing.
It could move both quadrupedally and bipedally; habitual speed and herd structure are not directly known.

presentation.heroLead: A large, broad-beaked duck-billed dinosaur from the Late Cretaceous of Alberta, known from many skulls and skeletons and from rare specimens preserving skin and a fleshy head comb.

animalParagraphs: Edmontosaurus regalis was one of the largest hadrosaurids, with adults around nine to twelve metres long. Its skull was long and low, ending in a broad, toothless beak, and behind the beak the jaws carried dental batteries of hundreds of closely packed teeth that formed a continuous grinding surface. Unlike its crested relatives it had no hollow bony crest.

The animal is known from many individuals of different sizes, so its growth is unusually well documented. Skull shape changed considerably as it grew, and some historic species names were founded on juveniles or on individuals of the closely related, later species Edmontosaurus annectens. This profile is scoped to E. regalis.

A specimen from the Wapiti Formation preserves the impression of a fleshy comb on top of the head, a structure that bones alone would never have revealed. Other specimens preserve patches of small, non-overlapping scales. Neither shows colour, and the comb's function is unknown.
animalHighlights: A broad, flattened beak backed by dental batteries with hundreds of teeth arranged in a grinding surface.
No bony crest, but one specimen preserves a soft, fleshy comb on top of the head.
A juvenile-to-adult growth series shows how the skull lengthened and deepened with age.

lifeCards.label: Feeding
lifeCards.level: Supported by dental batteries and wear
lifeCards.reason: Tooth wear and jaw mechanics show grinding of tough plant material. The particular plants eaten by E. regalis are not directly preserved.

lifeCards.label: Movement
lifeCards.reason: Hoof-like hands and strong hindlimbs allow both gaits; how often it used each, and its speed, are inferred.

lifeCards.label: Known size
lifeCards.reason: Lengths come from well-preserved adults; masses of several tonnes are model-based estimates.

lifeCards.label: Appearance
lifeCards.reason: Scale impressions and a fleshy head comb are preserved, but colour, pattern and the extent of soft structures over the rest of the body are not.

presentation.classificationSummary: Edmontosaurus is a saurolophine hadrosaurid, one of the flat-headed duck-billed dinosaurs that lacked the hollow crests of lambeosaurines. E. regalis is the type species; E. annectens from the latest Maastrichtian is a separate, later species.

related.reason: Compare with a solid-crested saurolophine from the same formation.
Compare with a hollow-crested lambeosaurine that shared the Horseshoe Canyon Formation.
Compare with the largest known hadrosaurid, a close relative from China.

questions.title: Which specimens belong to which species?
questions.copy: Several historic names and specimens need reassessment. Juvenile skulls in particular have been confused with separate species.

questions.title: Did all individuals have a comb?
questions.copy: The fleshy comb is known from one specimen. Whether it was present in both sexes or at all ages is unknown.

questions.title: Did it live in herds?
questions.copy: Bonebeds elsewhere show that Edmontosaurus could occur in large groups, but herd structure and social behaviour are inferred rather than observed.

review.ageReviewNote: The profile is scoped to E. regalis, primarily about 73-69 Ma; E. annectens extends the genus into the latest Maastrichtian but is taxonomically distinct.

panel.headline: Many skulls and skeletons, a growth series and rare soft-tissue impressions.
panel.standfirst: Edmontosaurus regalis is known from numerous skulls and substantial skeletons from Alberta, including the two type specimens described by Lawrence Lambe in 1917 and a specimen preserving skin and a fleshy comb. It is among the best-documented hadrosaurids.

coverage.label: Excellent
coverage.basis: Every skeletal region is known from multiple individuals of different growth stages, with complete skulls, near-complete skeletons and soft-tissue impressions.

knownRemains.title: What is actually preserved?
knownRemains.summary: Complete and partial skulls with dental batteries, full vertebral series, both girdles, complete limbs with hands and feet, juveniles through large adults, and impressions of scaly skin and a soft cranial comb.
knownRemains.note: Some historic specimens were assigned to other species or genera and still require reassessment; the broader genus, including E. annectens, adds famous mummified specimens from the United States that are not E. regalis.

materialGroups.label: Skull and jaws
materialGroups.value: Many complete and partial skulls with dental batteries and beaks, spanning juvenile to adult.

materialGroups.label: Vertebral column
materialGroups.value: Complete cervical, dorsal, sacral and caudal series with ossified tendons, ribs and chevrons in several individuals.

materialGroups.label: Girdles and limbs
materialGroups.value: Complete shoulder and hip girdles and all limb elements, including hooved hands and feet.

materialGroups.label: Exceptional preservation
materialGroups.value: Impressions of small scales and a fleshy head comb; no colour or gut contents are known for E. regalis.

specimenCards.description: A skull and partial skeleton collected by Levi Sternberg in 1912 from the Horseshoe Canyon Formation and described by Lambe in 1917, together with the paratype CMN 2289. Both are held by the Canadian Museum of Nature.

interpretation.label: Directly observed
interpretation.value: Numerous skulls and skeletons across growth stages, dental batteries with wear, scale impressions and a soft cranial comb.

interpretation.label: Scientific interpretation
interpretation.value: A large grinding herbivore able to walk on two or four legs, whose comb was probably a display structure and whose growth changed skull proportions markedly.

interpretation.label: Still unknown
interpretation.value: Colour, how widespread the comb was, herd structure, habitual gait and the correct species assignment of some historic specimens.
